rv.q: Matthew Warchus's moody and murky renovation is extremely digestible.

By staging it so effectively in pocket-sized form, Warchus may have inadvertently made a case for Martin Guerre as a minor piece rather than a rediscovered classic; it’s hard to imagine this iteration of the musical transitioning to a bigger stage.
Andrusier is such a powerful performer, her rendition of one of the show’s new songs, Someday, is a blast of such passion, that it is as if a new hero has arisen to take claim of this story.
New number Someday, sung with gusto by Andrusier, is the heart of the show.
What you’re left with is Leeds Mis, as a friend quipped.
I’m glad I’ve seen Martin Guerre — but, definitive or not, I found it intriguing rather than devastating, skilful more than soulful.
But it is, simply, not a great musical.
Indeed, it plays out like a pacy, screamy folk-horror, but one that takes itself far too seriously.
You betcha, without the tiniest soupçons of a doubt.
This trimmed-down revival makes a compelling case for a long-misunderstood work.
And yet, it still doesn’t quite earn its place among the golden greats.
So, this updated version's heart remains elusive, but its undeniable charm keeps our blood pumping.
The singing is great, but the tone is relentlessly dark, and you may struggle to follow the story.
This semi-staged production is an extraordinarily moving reimagining of the original musical.
For audiences willing to meet it on its own terms, the rewards are an evening of vital, immersive musical theatre that wears its Gallic heart proudly on its sleeve.
This stripped-down, minimalist Martin Guerre makes 90 minutes fly past in a frenetic blur.
I loved every minute, and thank you Mr Warchus, again.
The whole cast is fantastic; their voices are nothing short of angelic, and watching the play in the round really brings it all so very close.
Rob Howell’s stripped-back set and costumes pay dividends, pulling the focus away from aesthetics so the ears can concentrate on a songbook that charms at nearly every turn.
Ultimately, this production of Martin Guerre demonstrates just how powerful Boublil and Schönberg’s storytelling and music can be, even in a much more condensed form.
It was the immediacy of both the musical and the staging that made the evening so successful, meaning that in this format Martin Guerre may have found its sweet spot.
In its current form, it is still a thoroughly enjoyable watch with some stunning musical numbers and an incredible cast, led by a faultless performance from Liv Andrusier.
It’s not that Martin Guerre is bad at all, it just struggles to work out that final step from goodness to greatness.
However, the repeated waving of large flags feels counterproductive in a production striving to emerge from Les Misérables’ shadow.
This is truly a magnificent show.
There is still a great deal to love about Martin Guerre, and it remains an amazing musical.
It is gripping in its own way, but it is neither epic, nor does it quite have the intimacy of a love story.
Albeit visually enticing, Warchus's take is unlikely to bring so many tears to the viewers' eyes (removing that tune might have something to do with it).
Ultimately, this is a respectable, well-intentioned production that struggles with its material.

cn.t: Critics find this radically reworked Martin Guerre well-sung and intimately staged, but most agree it still falls short of Les Mis heights. The 90-minute reimagining earns praise for strong performances, yet struggles with emotional depth and identity.
